articles.title: How I added English to my solo-dev Unity MMO without touching 130 UI files
articles.excerpt: My game, Battle of Pirates, is a free online pirate MMO for Windows: real-time naval PvP, fleets, fortress sieges, boss events. I build it alone in Turkey, so for two years every string in the game wa…
articles.body: My game, Battle of Pirates , is a free online pirate MMO for Windows: real-time naval PvP, fleets, fortress sieges, boss events. I build it alone in Turkey, so for two years every string in the game was hardcoded Turkish. Players here search for it as an online korsan oyunu , and that was fine until the game started showing up on itch.io and IndieDB and international players arrived. The problem: about 1,700 unique UI strings across 130 C# files , all built in code ( text.text = "AYARLAR" ), plus hundreds of server messages sent from Node.js. Wrapping every literal in a T("...") call would touch every file and risk breaking a live game.

articles.title: Recuerdos.local: An Offline Ofrenda & Memory Weaver
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine I built Recuerdos.local, a fully offline, voice-interactive digital ofrenda (altar) and memory archivis…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built I built Recuerdos.local , a fully offline, voice-interactive digital ofrenda (altar) and memory archivist. It acts as a gentle conversational companion that interviews you about a lost loved one, transcribes your stories, and weaves them into a beautiful, static digital remembrance—extracting favorite foods, songs, and core memories along the way. The inspiration came from my family's Día de los Muertos traditions. We spend hours telling stories about those who have passed, but those oral histories fade. I wanted a way to preserve them without inviting corporate data-mining into our most intimate moments of grief and remembrance.
articles.author: sujal chandel

articles.title: How I built a countdown & days-since tracker with React 19, Supabase and Vercel
articles.excerpt: I wanted a place to count down to things – a trip, a birthday, a deadline – and to count up from things, like the day I started a habit. Most countdown sites I tried were full of ads or wanted an acco…
articles.body: I wanted a place to count down to things – a trip, a birthday, a deadline – and to count up from things, like the day I started a habit. Most countdown sites I tried were full of ads or wanted an account before I could type a date. So I built my own: CountMyDays. It's a solo side project, and this post is about how it's put together and a few things that bit me along the way. The stack React 19 + Vite + TypeScript for the frontend Supabase for Postgres, magic-link auth and Realtime Vercel for hosting Tailwind for styling, and a service worker so it installs as a PWA and works offline Nothing exotic. The interesting parts are in how data moves between "guest" and "signed in", and in how the timer stays accurate. Guest first, account later I didn't want a sign-up wall.
articles.author: CountMyDays

articles.title: How often does an LLM name a poker hand it doesn't hold? I counted for two models
articles.excerpt: My blunders endpoint flags GLM 4.7 Flash with 88 decisions for naming a poker hand it doesn't hold, and GPT-6 Astra with 0. I wanted to know whether the 88 was real, so I read some of them. People pla…
articles.body: My blunders endpoint flags GLM 4.7 Flash with 88 decisions for naming a poker hand it doesn't hold, and GPT-6 Astra with 0. I wanted to know whether the 88 was real, so I read some of them. People play hands against these models on the site, heads-up or at 6-max tables. Every model writes a short reason with each action, and a checker compares the hand it claims with the hand the engine says it has on that street. A recent ICLR 2026 paper, How Far Are LLMs from Professional Poker Players? , lists three problems with how models reason. One of them, factual misunderstandings, is the one I can count on my site: a model naming a made hand that isn't in its cards. What gets counted The checker flags a decision when the reason claims a made hand stronger than the engine's.

articles.body: RecallAI: Building a Second Memory with Computer Vision at Cal Hacks 13.0 This is a submission for the MLH x DEV Writing Challenge. What I Built What if AI could remember the things we forget? At Cal Hacks 13.0, my team and I built RecallAI, an AI-powered visual memory assistant designed to help people remember where they last saw their belongings and retrieve those memories through natural conversation. We’ve all experienced that frustrating moment when we can’t find our keys, headphones, wallet, or something else important. Instead of searching everywhere, imagine simply asking: “Hey RecallAI, where did I last see my AirPods?” And getting a response like: “Your AirPods were last seen on your desk 23 minutes ago.” That’s the idea behind RecallAI.

articles.body: A pattern like this ships in real projects every day: ^(?\[(?:[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)\])|^(?[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)\s*=\s*(?"(?:[^"\\]|\\.)*"|'(?:[^'\\]|\\.)*'|[^#\n]*)\s*(?:#.*)?$ An INI-line parser: a section header or a key–value pair, three quoting modes for the value, trailing comments. Perfectly readable — to the person who wrote it, today. Come back in three months, or hand it to a teammate, and the review comment is always the same: what does this actually match? Formatting solves this the way it's solved for every other language. The same pattern, laid out by structure: ^ (? \[(?:[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)\]) | ^ (? [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*) \s* = \s* (? articles.title: NASA ends Swift space telescope mission after failed rescue attempt
articles.excerpt: NASA has officially ended the mission of its Swift Observatory, after a private satellite failed to meet up with the aging spacecraft in orbit.
articles.body: NASA has officially ended the mission of its Swift space telescope, after a private satellite failed in its bold bid to rescue the aging spacecraft. That rescue mission was led by the Arizona company Katalyst Space Technologies, whose LINK spacecraft tried to meet up with Swift this summer to boost its orbit. That didn't work out, however, so Swift continues its fall back toward Earth. The telescope is expected to reenter Earth's atmosphere "in the next few weeks," NASA said in a statement on Friday (Oct. 23). That statement served primarily to announce the end of the Swift mission after more than 20 very productive years. The telescope launched to Earth orbit in November 2004, tasked with studying gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) — the most powerful explosions in the cosmos.

articles.excerpt: Members of the media are invited to tour a new lunar landing simulator at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley on Thursday, Oct. 29, and Friday, Oct. 30.
articles.body: 2 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Members of the media are invited to tour a new lunar landing simulation at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley on Thursday, Oct. 29, and Friday, Oct. 30. Using a combination of in-house and partner motion-based simulators, NASA is giving astronauts and engineering support teams simulated experiences before crew members pilot commercial human landing systems to the surface of the Moon. Through the Artemis program, NASA is targeting the next lunar landing in 2028. During the tour, media will have an opportunity to participate in a Vertical Motion Simulator ride-along and interview subject matter experts. Media interested in participating should RSVP by Tuesday, Oct.

articles.title: Record breaker! Astronomers spot powerful cosmic explosion that lasted 27 days
articles.excerpt: Astronomers have spotted a remarkable gamma-ray burst that's a real Incredible Hulk compared to other cosmic explosions of the same type.
articles.body: Astronomers have spotted a remarkable gamma-ray burst (GRB) that's a real Incredible Hulk compared to other cosmic explosions of the same type. What makes this GRB so special is the fact that the central engine powering it remained active for around 27 days, flaring in X-rays following the initial blast. That's 20 days longer than the longest previous GRB on record. This record-breaking burst — which is designated GRB 220706A and was spotted on July 6, 2022 — is even more exciting because scientists don't know what the central engine powering it actually is. "In a nutshell, GRB 220706A is an extremely late X-ray flare.
